name: Cryptic crossword No 29,858
preamble: Eleven clues consist of wordplay only, their entries defined by the puzzle itself.

clue.text: Timothy and Bridget met and stripped

indicators.note: people who meet come together, so the two kept parts are joined end to end
stripping takes the covering away, so each name loses part of itself and only a portion is kept

blocks.note: the final two letters of the name, where it meets the next one
the opening four letters of the second name

explanation.surface: Two people called Timothy and Bridget met up and undressed together.
explanation.walkthrough: Written as one run, timothyBRIDget, the meeting point holds HYBRID once the outer letters are stripped away. There is no definition: the puzzle's theme, CROSS, defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid is the offspring of two different breeds or species, which is exactly what a cross means in breeding.

clue.text: Bully is one acting to grab that which belongs to me

indicators.note: grabbing takes something into one's hands, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: someone who acts or does things
the possessive pronoun for something of mine

explanation.surface: A bully is someone who acts to snatch whatever is mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully' is a verb here, matching the verb answer; the possessive phrase is a long-winded way of saying one short pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: To domineer is to rule over others arrogantly and overbearingly, the same behaviour as to bully them.

clue.text: Thrilled at first quarter growth

indicators.note: the opening fourth of a word is its first quarter, so only that leading portion is kept

blocks.note: first letters only: the word has eight, so its first quarter is the first two
a small growth on the skin

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted with three months of business growth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First quarter' sounds like a financial period, but it means the first quarter of the word before it. There is no definition: the theme word CROSS defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To cross someone is to oppose or frustrate their plans, which is what thwarting them means.

clue.text: Balloon is no fun from the outset, and others go up

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so only the opening letter of each word is kept
in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, the other way round

blocks.note: the opening letters of these three words
et al, Latin shorthand for 'and others'

explanation.surface: A complaint that ballooning is dull while everyone else gets to rise into the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balloon' looks like the noun for a hot-air balloon, but it is the verb, meaning to swell.
explanation.definitionFit: To balloon is to swell up with air or grow rapidly, the same sense as to inflate.

clue.text: Setting off, parking Tesla to have something to eat

indicators.note: to park something is to leave it behind, so a letter is dropped and left out
something gone off is spoiled or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: A driver sets off on a journey, parks the Tesla car and stops for a bite.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesla is not the car maker but the scientific unit, whose symbol is T; one T leaves SETTING before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingest is to take food or drink into the body, so it amounts to eating or consuming a meal.

clue.text: Dancers in mid-step …

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it
the mid part of a word is its centre, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of this four-letter word
ravers are people who dance at raves

explanation.surface: Dancers caught in the middle of a step, with the ellipsis leading on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis only links the surface to 11 down; the wordplay stands alone. The theme word CROSS is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To cross a space is to go from one side to the other, which is what traversing it means.

clue.text: One’s struck by shattering of only hope

indicators.note: shattering breaks something into pieces, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: 'by' as in multiplication, three by four, written with the times sign X
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is devastated when their last remaining hope is dashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One’s struck' reads as someone being hit emotionally, but it means an instrument that is played by striking it. 'By' gives X, as in a room measuring ten by twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: A xylophone is a percussion instrument whose wooden bars are hit with mallets to sound notes.

clue.text: Gary Coleman’s last performance?

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
a performance puts on a show with things worked differently, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A question about the final acting role of Gary Coleman, the American child star of Diff'rent Strokes.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous name is split: the first name is taken whole and only the surname's end is used. The theme word CROSS defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross is an everyday British word for annoyed or bad-tempered, the same as angry.

clue.text: Scientists propose more scientists retract first

indicators.note: to retract is to draw back, so the letters run backwards
placed first means this part comes at the front of the answer

blocks.note: the Royal Institution, a British body of scientists
the Royal Institution again
to table a motion is to put it forward for discussion

explanation.surface: A row between research teams: one group makes a proposal, another withdraws its earlier one.
explanation.walkthrough: RI is the Royal Institution, a London scientific society. To table a motion, in British usage, is to put it forward. The theme word CROSS defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross as an adjective means bad-tempered or easily annoyed, the same mood as irritable.

clue.text: Haul bundled crops with bits falling off

indicators.note: pieces falling off the edges means the outermost letters are lost

blocks.note: sheaves are bundles of cut corn or wheat

explanation.surface: A farmer lugs bundles of harvested crops, bits dropping off as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: Both ends of SHEAVES drop away.
explanation.definitionFit: To haul something is to pull or lift it with great effort, which is also what heaving it means.

clue.text: … seen during Bank Holiday …

indicators.note: something seen during a period appears within it, so the letters sit inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Something spotted over a public holiday weekend, continuing the chain of ellipses.
explanation.walkthrough: A bank holiday is a British public holiday. The answer hides in bANK Holiday; the theme word CROSS is its definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ankh is an ancient Egyptian looped cross, a symbol of life, so it is a kind of cross.

clue.text: A time to have chocolate-covered dates? Quite the reverse!

definitions.text: A time to have chocolate-covered dates? Quite the reverse!

blocks.clueFragment: A time to have chocolate-covered dates?
blocks.note: surface reading: a season for eating dates, the fruit, dipped in chocolate
setter's reading: the dates on the calendar cover the chocolates, each hidden behind a numbered door

explanation.surface: A season for indulging in chocolate-coated dates, the fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Dates are calendar days, not fruit: in the weeks before Christmas, a calendar has a little door for each date with a chocolate behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The season leading up to Christmas is when children open a calendar door each day for a chocolate.

clue.text: On a crest, fur, metal, splash of colour? Amazingly, true!

indicators.note: a splash is just a little dash, so only the opening letter is kept
something amazing is astonishing and unexpected, so the letters are turned into a surprising new order

blocks.note: a common metal
the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: An excited observation that a coat of arms features fur, metal and a bit of colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The list reads as one heraldic description, but 'metal' and 'colour' are wordplay while 'On a crest, fur' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry the tinctures are the colours, metals and furs used on a coat of arms, so a fur is one example.

clue.text: Sum up about two seconds’ talk

blocks.note: to sum numbers is to add them
re means concerning or about
S is the abbreviation for second, twice

explanation.surface: Summarising what was said in a speech that lasted only a couple of seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sum up' wants to mean summarise, but here it is plain arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is a formal speech given to an audience, so it is a talk.

clue.text: … game, where girl goes across line

indicators.note: one thing going across another spans it on both sides, so it encloses what it crosses

blocks.note: a girl's name
Go is the Japanese board game
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: At the end of the ellipsis chain, a game in which a girl crosses a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' looks like part of the picture but just gives L. The theme word CROSS is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Crosswise means running slantwise across, from corner to corner, which is a diagonal direction.

clue.text: Rests up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from bottom to top, the opposite way

blocks.note: naps are short rests

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rests up' looks like a phrase meaning recuperates, but 'up' is the turnaround signal. The theme word CROSS is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge that crosses a river is said to span it, stretching from bank to bank.

clue.text: Space not quite enough for a big red book?

indicators.note: falling just short means the word ends one letter early

blocks.note: The dictionary favoured by crossword setters, a large red volume

explanation.surface: A shelf without enough room for a large red volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The big red book is the Chambers Dictionary, the British reference that cryptic setters lean on; cut short, it loses its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamber is an enclosed room or cavity, so it is a space, as in a chamber of the heart.

clue.text: Twinkling girls that might be described as ‘thick and sweet’

definitions.text: that might be described as ‘thick and sweet’

blocks.note: a twinkling is a moment, shortened to mo
lasses are girls, especially in Scotland and northern England

explanation.surface: Bright-eyed young women whom someone might call thick and sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twinkling' looks like a description of the girls, but it is a noun: in the twinkling of an eye means in a moment. The definition describes a substance, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: Molasses is the dark, viscous syrup left over from refining sugar, so it is notably syrupy and sugary.

clue.text: Silly, like in fifth grade?

blocks.note: 'as in' introduces an example, just as 'like' does
taken as written
grades run A, B, C, D, E, so the fifth is E

explanation.surface: Behaviour so silly it belongs to a schoolchild of about ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifth grade' suggests an American school year, but it means the fifth mark on an A-to-E scale.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means extremely foolish, literally like an ass or donkey, so it is a strong synonym.

clue.text: Those north of Zimbabwe and South Africa going round South Namib

indicators.note: going round turns things about, so these letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: ZA is South Africa's international vehicle and internet code
S for South, then the desert's name as written

explanation.surface: A geography note on the peoples bordering Zimbabwe and South Africa, near the Namib Desert.
explanation.walkthrough: Zimbabwe belongs to the definition, not the wordplay; 'and' separates them. South Africa's code ZA starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Zambia lies directly over Zimbabwe's northern border, so its citizens live there.

clue.text: Half-upset, was suffused with passion

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and only half of the word is turned the other way

blocks.note: someone burning with desire is filled with passion

explanation.surface: Someone who was partly troubled was also overcome with passion.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second half, the last three letters, turns around. The theme defines the answer: a cross to bear is a burden.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy trouble one must endure is called a cross to bear, after the cross carried by Jesus, so it is a load.

clue.text: Soup with crust of skin covering

indicators.note: a crust is the outer layer around something, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a pelt is an animal's skin
Soup is the setter's pseudonym, so the setter refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: A bowl of soup that has formed a skin on top.
explanation.walkthrough: Soup is this puzzle's setter, so the word stands for the setter, ME. 'Skin' on soup suggests the film on top, but it means an animal hide.
explanation.definitionFit: A pelmet is a narrow board or fabric strip fitted above a window to conceal the curtain fittings.

clue.text: Number 1 against seeds in third and fourth place

indicators.note: the letters standing in positions three and four are kept and the rest discarded

blocks.note: doing a number one is a child's euphemism for urinating
V for versus
the third and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A tennis draw: the top seed faces the seeds ranked third and fourth.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis picture hides a lavatory joke: number one is nursery slang for urine. The theme word CROSS defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross as an adjective means irritated or annoyed, the same as being peeved.

clue.text: Ate out, went and got topless

indicators.note: without a top, so in a down entry the uppermost letter goes

blocks.note: to fetch something is to go and get it

explanation.surface: Someone dined at a restaurant, went off and got their top off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ate out' looks like dining at a restaurant, but it means corroded, as acid eats away a metal plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid etches metal by eating into its surface, so to etch is literally to corrode away.

clue.text: Poor excuse?

blocks.note: first meaning: wretched or pitiful, as in a pitiful state
second meaning: what you say for 'pardon?' or 'excuse me?'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor excuse' reads as a feeble justification; split, the two words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an adjective for something pitiful or wretched, and an interjection asking someone to repeat themselves.

clue.text: In brief: about time

blocks.note: taken as written
terse means brief and to the point
C for circa, about
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A terse note, in brief, about the time of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In brief' sounds like 'to summarise', but each word is its own piece. The theme word CROSS defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Two roads that cross meet and pass through each other, which is what intersecting means.

clue.text: Mind thematic character’s greenery

blocks.note: to mind something is to care about it
the letter that looks like the theme, a cross

explanation.surface: A warning to look after a certain personality's plants.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle's theme is CROSS, and X is the letter shaped like one.
explanation.definitionFit: Carex is the botanical genus of sedges, grassy plants, so it is a kind of vegetation; the definition is loose.

clue.text: Showing age, uncomfortably nude, I covered wiener, backing indoors

indicators.note: something uncomfortable sits awkwardly, so these letters are put out of their order
with this letter covered up it can no longer be seen, so it drops out
backing means moving backwards, so the letters run the other way
being indoors means being inside a building, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ageing person, awkwardly naked, covers up out of modesty while retreating into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: A wiener is a hot-dog sausage, or slang for a penis, which explains the coy covering in the surface. Its I is removed, the rest reversed and placed within the rearranged NUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something never refreshed or restored keeps the wear of the years, so it looks old and tired.
